Get started with zujose

Source: vignettes/articles/zujose.Rmd
zujose.Rmd

zujose signs, verifies, encrypts and decrypts JOSE objects. This article walks through the pieces in the order you meet them: keys, JSON Web Tokens, signatures and encryption underneath, and reading a token you have not checked yet.

library(zujose)

The vocabulary

JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) is a family of standards:

  • a JWS (RFC 7515) is a signed payload;
  • a JWE (RFC 7516) is an encrypted payload;
  • a JWK (RFC 7517) is a key written as JSON, and a JWK Set is a list of them;
  • a JWT (RFC 7519) is a set of claims, such as who the token is about and when it expires, carried as the payload of a JWS or a JWE.

Each comes in a compact serialization, the familiar xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz, and a JSON one. RFC 7518 lists the algorithms. zujose names each function after the object it works on: jwt_encode(), jws_sign(), jwe_decrypt(), jwk_generate(). The token or payload is the first argument and the key the second.

Keys

A key is a jwk. A symmetric key, of type oct, is a secret shared by whoever signs and whoever verifies. Generate one for the algorithm you mean to use, and it is the right length:

hmac <- jwk_generate("oct", alg = "HS256", kid = "hmac-1")
hmac
#> <jwk> oct, 256 bits
#>   kid "hmac-1"
#>   alg HS256
#>   private: yes (not shown)

Printing never shows the secret. An existing secret, as raw bytes, is wrapped with jwk_oct(). A password is not a key: turn it into one with a key derivation function, or use PBES2 encryption, which does that for you.

Public-key algorithms need a key pair. zujose makes RSA keys and elliptic-curve keys on P-256, P-384, P-521 and X25519:

signer <- jwk_generate("EC", crv = "P-256", alg = "ES256", kid = "ec-1")
signer
#> <jwk> EC, 256 bits
#>   kid "ec-1"
#>   alg ES256
#>   private: yes (not shown)

as_jwk() reads a key from JWK text or from PEM, and jwk_json() and jwk_pem() write one. Both write only the public part unless you ask for the private one:

jwk_json(signer)
#> [1] "{\"kty\":\"EC\",\"crv\":\"P-256\",\"x\":\"wWYFybiNa_CNW1t4C29RFS6_YKlMOA-5qvJi3DQDaR4\",\"y\":\"Fuq5c3nvU1LbYS_i8Yd5h3V7xiBmTyOTBGxjnFXXYFw\",\"kid\":\"ec-1\",\"alg\":\"ES256\"}"

A key set holds several keys. Its JWK Set text is what an identity provider publishes, and what a client reads to verify the provider’s tokens:

keys <- jwk_set(signer, jwk_generate("RSA", alg = "RS256", kid = "rsa-1"))
keys
#> <jwk_set> 2 keys
#>   EC "ec-1" ES256
#>   RSA "rsa-1" RS256
cat(jwk_json(keys))
#> {"keys":[{"kty":"EC","crv":"P-256","x":"wWYFybiNa_CNW1t4C29RFS6_YKlMOA-5qvJi3DQDaR4","y":"Fuq5c3nvU1LbYS_i8Yd5h3V7xiBmTyOTBGxjnFXXYFw","kid":"ec-1","alg":"ES256"},{"kty":"RSA","n":"5f_GH1W860ZQZJwTb1_WCNoK8KhPCZpr_JkCa9wEIwTSM3ciSf1oDVLLE-HeP08GSID2Yt8jSmEToCBwIKp0dc6RuK9fhUUu7PKlfSC_jpLmb93nzLsSY1ujQlHpl8-T6cGwc04GYsqw5fvrh6BSudjWutRHR7LNGcq4CQBFTEjbYuG1Xn4n23z0QVVklB5bsw0FDJQ5hQRZRlklUp0_Z2TunqrtiaunXs65DallEE5mMjEriS0CrHSYOUwffOfTa7GMT6tLhRFBR2cq_U4BYKvwM--6UhYBdrhDtKDJBo2mmDm2HRSPP0BfscnR1aTcICC5u-7zZvp7w4M2qFe4zw","e":"AQAB","kid":"rsa-1","alg":"RS256"}]}

as_jwk_set() reads that text back. A key in a set is picked by the kid in a token’s header. Two more tools help with naming keys: jwk_with_kid() names a key by its RFC 7638 thumbprint, which needs no registry, and jwk_thumbprint() computes the thumbprint itself.

Keys live in ordinary R memory, which R can copy and cannot wipe. See the “Secrets in memory” section of ?jwk_oct for what that means.

JSON Web Tokens

jwt_encode() signs a list of claims. expires_in sets exp, and iat is added for you:

jwt <- jwt_encode(
  list(iss = "https://auth.example", sub = "user-17", aud = "orders-api"),
  signer,
  expires_in = 600
)

jwt_decode() checks the token in one call. You say which algorithms you accept; there is no default, so a token cannot choose a weaker one for you. The key must fit the algorithm. Then the claims are checked: exp is required by default, nbf and iat are checked when present, with a leeway of 60 seconds, and audience, issuer and subject are matched when you give them:

claims <- jwt_decode(
  jwt,
  jwk_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  audience = "orders-api",
  issuer = "https://auth.example"
)
claims
#> <jwt_claims> verified ES256, key "ec-1"
#>   iss: "https://auth.example"
#>   sub: "user-17"
#>   aud: "orders-api"
#>   exp: 2026-11-03 15:27:50 UTC
#>   iat: 2026-11-03 15:17:50 UTC

claims takes per-claim expectations, as a value or as a function that must return TRUE, and validate takes one function of all the claims:

jwt_decode(
  jwt,
  jwk_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  audience = "orders-api",
  claims = list(sub = function(sub) startsWith(sub, "user-"))
)$sub
#> [1] "user-17"

When the same checks apply to every request, jwt_decoder() fixes them once and returns a function of the token:

check <- jwt_decoder(
  key = jwk_public(keys),
  algorithms = c("ES256", "RS256"),
  audience = "orders-api",
  issuer = "https://auth.example"
)
check(jwt)$sub
#> [1] "user-17"

When a check fails

Every error is a condition whose class says what failed, all inheriting from zujose_error. Catch the class, not the message:

expired <- jwt_encode(list(sub = "user-17"), hmac, expires_in = -3600)
tryCatch(
  jwt_decode(expired, hmac, algorithms = "HS256"),
  zujose_expired_error = function(e) paste("expired at", e$time)
)
#> [1] "expired at 2026-11-03 14:17:50"

A token signed with an algorithm you did not allow is a policy error, raised before any cryptography is done:

jwt_decode(jwt, jwk_public(signer), algorithms = "RS256")
#> Error in `jwt_decode()`:
#> ! The token's algorithm is not in `algorithms`.

?zujose_error lists every class and the fields each carries.

Signatures: JWS

A JWT is a JWS whose payload is a JSON object. jws_sign() and jws_verify() sign and verify any payload, given as a string or as raw bytes:

token <- jws_sign("Order 1042 shipped.", hmac)
verified <- jws_verify(token, hmac, algorithms = "HS256")
rawToChar(verified$payload)
#> [1] "Order 1042 shipped."

format = "flattened" or "general" writes the JSON serialization, and several signers, made with jws_signer(), sign one payload together:

token <- jws_sign(
  "Order 1042 shipped.",
  list(jws_signer(hmac), jws_signer(signer)),
  format = "general"
)

By default every signature must verify. A recipient that holds only one of the keys asks for any one signature instead:

jws_verify(
  token,
  jwk_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  require = "any"
)$kid
#> [1] "ec-1"

Encryption: JWE

A JWE is encrypted in two layers: a random content encryption key encrypts the payload (enc), and the key management algorithm (alg) delivers that key to the recipient. To encrypt for a public key, use the recipient’s public key:

recipient <- jwk_generate("RSA", kid = "rsa-enc")
jwe <- jwe_encrypt(
  "card ending 4242",
  jwk_public(recipient),
  alg = "RSA-OAEP-256",
  enc = "A256GCM"
)

Decrypting names both the key management and the content encryption algorithms you accept:

out <- jwe_decrypt(
  jwe,
  recipient,
  algorithms = "RSA-OAEP-256",
  encryptions = "A256GCM"
)
rawToChar(out$plaintext)
#> [1] "card ending 4242"

Every decryption failure raises zujose_decrypt_error with the same message, whatever went wrong, so a failure tells an attacker nothing about the key.

A password encrypts through PBES2, which derives the key from it. Give the password to jwk_oct() as bytes:

password <- jwk_oct(charToRaw("correct horse battery staple"))
jwe <- jwe_encrypt(
  "backup notes",
  password,
  alg = "PBES2-HS256+A128KW",
  enc = "A128GCM"
)
rawToChar(jwe_decrypt(jwe, password, "PBES2-HS256+A128KW", "A128GCM")$plaintext)
#> [1] "backup notes"

Encrypted JWTs

A JWT can be signed and then encrypted, so that only the recipient can read the claims. Compose the two steps:

nested <- jwt_encode(list(sub = "user-17"), signer, expires_in = 600) |>
  jwe_encrypt(
    jwk_public(recipient),
    alg = "RSA-OAEP-256",
    enc = "A256GCM",
    header = list(cty = "JWT")
  )

jwt_decode() accepts an encrypted JWT only when you say how to decrypt it, with jwe_decryption(). Without it, a JWE where a signed token was expected is refused:

jwt_decode(
  nested,
  jwk_public(signer),
  algorithms = "ES256",
  decrypt = jwe_decryption(recipient, "RSA-OAEP-256", "A256GCM")
)$sub
#> [1] "user-17"

Reading a token without checking it

Sometimes you need to look inside a token before you can check it, for example to read its kid or iss and choose a key. jose_peek() decodes every part of a token and verifies nothing:

jose_peek(jwt)
#> <jose_unverified> JWS, compact serialization
#> ! Not verified: nothing here can be trusted.
#> Header:
#>   alg: "ES256"
#>   kid: "ec-1"
#>   typ: "JWT"
#> Claims:
#>   iss: "https://auth.example"
#>   sub: "user-17"
#>   aud: "orders-api"
#>   exp: 1793719670
#>   iat: 1793719070
#> Signature: 64 bytes

Its result is classed jose_unverified and says so. Use it to decide which key or policy to apply, never to decide whether to trust the token.

Limits and supported algorithms

Every function that reads a token checks its size, its header, the number of signatures or recipients and the PBES2 iteration count against jose_limits() before decoding anything. The defaults suit ordinary tokens; raise them only for a source you trust.

zujose_info() lists every algorithm and whether the installed zucrypt provides it:

head(zujose_info())
#>   algorithm      kind available zucrypt
#> 1     HS256 signature      TRUE   0.1.0
#> 2     HS384 signature      TRUE   0.1.0
#> 3     HS512 signature      TRUE   0.1.0
#> 4     RS256 signature      TRUE   0.4.0
#> 5     RS384 signature      TRUE   0.4.0
#> 6     RS512 signature      TRUE   0.4.0
